extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating patent-eligibility of nature-based products
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 'markedly different characteristics' comparison used to decide whether a claimed nature-based product is a product-of-nature exception for patent eligibility. Covers when to perform the analysis, how to select natural counterparts, which characteristics to compare, and how to evaluate whether differences are 'marked.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a markedly different characteristic on eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception (such as a law of nature or abstract idea, or a different natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., a claim to “a Lactobacillus bacterium”), once a markedly different characteristic in that product is shown, no further analysis would be necessary for eligibility because no product of nature exception is recited (i.e., Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including limitations in addition to the nature-based product, examiners should consider whether the claim recites another exception and thus requires further eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a nature-based product can be claimed by itself or as one or more limitations of a claim, care should be taken not to overly extend the analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception. If the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (for example due to some human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: How to apply the analysis when the claim is to a nature-based product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claim is to a nature-based product by itself (e.g., a claim to “a Lactobacillus bacterium”), apply the analysis to the entire product. Where the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components (e.g., “a probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk”), apply the analysis to the resultant nature-based combination rather than component parts. Where the claim is to a nature-based product in combination with non-nature based elements (e.g., a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions), apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to the nature-based product limitation; container and instructions are evaluated separately in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). (Cites: Chakrabarty; Funk Bros.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of product-by-process claims in the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a product-by-process claim (e.g., a cloned farm animal produced by a nuclear transfer cloning method), the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart. See MPEP § 2113 for more information on product-by-process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When process claims are and are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general rule is that a process claim is not subject to the markedly different analysis for nature-based products used in the process because the analysis of a process claim should focus on the active steps rather than products used. Examples exist where courts did not apply the analysis to process claims (e.g., cryopreserving hepatocytes). However, where a process claim is drafted so that there is no substantive difference from a product claim (i.e., the claim effectively focuses on the product), the claim is subject to the markedly different analysis (examples: 'a method of providing an apple'; claims to detecting cffDNA held directed to the cffDNA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the claimed nature-based product because the analysis compares the claimed product to its counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, that natural thing is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A's counterpart is acid A). The counterpart should be considered in its natural state but do not confuse the counterpart with other material that may occur naturally with or adjacent to it (e.g., a gene vs the whole chromosome). When there are multiple counterparts, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart; in some cases the examiner should select the closest counterpart based on expertise. When the claimed product is a combination with no natural counterpart, the closest counterparts may be the individual components (e.g., a mixture of bacterial species compared to each species as it occurs in nature). If a claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a 'best practice' for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to assist applicant responses and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the characteristics of the claimed product to be compared to the counterpart; appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners identify characteristics by looking at what is recited in the claim language and what is encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation of the nature-based product. A characteristic may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name indicating structural features) or derived from the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies a particular nucleotide sequence and encoded protein). Characteristics can be expressed as structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of the types of characteristics courts consider when determining whether there is a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities (e.g., protein-encoding information; binding ability; infectivity; ability to degrade hydrocarbons; therapeutic functions), chemical and physical properties (e.g., alkalinity; ductility/malleability), phenotype including functional and structural characteristics (e.g., shape, size, color, behavior), and structure and form whether chemical, genetic, or physical (e.g., presence of plasmids; chemical crystalline form; nucleotide sequence; genotype). Specific case citations accompany many examples (Myriad, Ambry Genetics, Chakrabarty, Parke-Davis, Marden, Roslin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether a characteristic is 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed product's characteristics to the counterpart to determine whether they are 'markedly different.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and that change came about or was produced by the inventor’s efforts or influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic so the claimed product is not a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to have markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples illustrating products that were held to have markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: a genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and the ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons was found markedly different and eligible. Myriad: a full-length cDNA (BRCA1) retaining exons but lacking introns was structurally distinct from the natural gene and held not a product of nature. These examples illustrate that either changed structure or changed function (or both) can support a marked difference when the change is produced by human intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples illustrating products found to be products of nature because they lacked markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated gene sequences that differ only by isolation (loss of chromosomal covalent bonds) but are otherwise identical to natural genes were not markedly different. Ambry Genetics: synthetic primers corresponding to natural nucleotide sequences lacked markedly different structure and function (primer binding is innate), thus they were products of nature. In re Marden: ductility of vanadium is inherent and not conferred by a new combination. Roslin: cloned animals that are genetic copies lacked markedly different characteristics; alleged phenotypic differences not claimed could not make them markedly different. These examples underscore that incidental differences, innate functions, or unclaimed phenotypic variations do not establish marked difference.
